proof.claim:
The node-agent maintenance loop must actually reclaim space, not merely start.

WHY THIS EXISTS. etcd-backend-does-not-ratchet asserts defrag_scheduled=true,
which becomes true the moment the loop logs etcd.maintenance_started at boot.
On the first cluster built with the fix, that assertion passed while the
measured reality was:

    loops_started: 6, defrags_run: 0, total_freed_bytes: 0

The backend sat at 79 MB against a 256 MB floor, so the pass had only ever
skipped. A loop that starts, skips forever, and reclaims nothing satisfies the
scheduled check exactly like a working one — the same shape as every other
defect in the 2026-08-16 chain: a check that cannot fail is indistinguishable
from one that passes.

This scenario closes that gap by making the condition real. It writes enough
data to push the backend past the maintenance floor, deletes it, and compacts
— leaving a large file that is mostly free pages, which is precisely the state
the outage lived in. Compaction never shrinks the file; only a defrag returns
the space to the filesystem. Then it waits for a maintenance turn and asserts
the loop did its job.

WHY THE WAIT IS LONG. The pass is round-robin over the sorted member list, so
exactly one member is eligible per 10-minute interval — that is the property
that stops a defrag from taking out quorum by pausing several members at once.
Any single node therefore waits up to memberCount intervals for its own turn,
but SOME node is eligible every interval, and all members replicate the same
data so every backend grows together. 13 minutes guarantees at least one turn
has come and gone.

Covered invariant: the fix for
etcd.backend_ratchets_because_nothing_defragments must be observed working,
not merely observed to be present.
